title: About SkyBlink & SPHEREx
intro: SkyBlink makes NASA's all-sky infrared survey SPHEREx easy to explore for everyone — from curious beginners to citizen scientists hunting brown dwarfs.

sections.spherexBody: NASA's SPHEREx space telescope surveys the entire sky in 102 infrared wavelength channels roughly every 6 months, making it ideal for spotting cool brown dwarfs and changing stars.
sections.motionBody: Nearby stars and brown dwarfs appear to drift across background galaxies over months and years because of proper motion and Earth's orbital parallax.
sections.brownDwarfsTitle: What are brown dwarfs & Planet X?
sections.brownDwarfsBody: Brown dwarfs are 'failed stars' too cool to shine brightly in visible light, so they glow mainly in the infrared. Searching for faint, fast-moving infrared sources could reveal undiscovered nearby brown dwarfs — or even distant solar system worlds.
sections.artifactsBody: Cosmic rays, hot pixels, and detector edges can mimic bright dots. Real objects repeat smoothly across dates and align with expected sky motion.

practice.title: Quick training: Spot the real signal
practice.subtitle: Step through the 4 simulated epochs below and classify what you see.
practice.tryAgain: Not quite — look at how the dot behaves across all 4 epochs.

1.title: Example A: Gradual shift
1.explanation: The source moves steadily pixel by pixel across consecutive epochs while background stars stay fixed — a classic brown dwarf or nearby star signature.

2.title: Example B: Brightness pulse
2.explanation: The star never moves from its coordinates, yet its brightness rises and fades smoothly across epochs — typical of a variable star like R Draconis.

3.title: Example C: Single-frame flash
3.explanation: A sharp dot appears in only one epoch and vanishes completely in the others — likely a cosmic ray hit or hot pixel artifact, not a real celestial object.
